frozen_original.title: DOJ Drops Defense of Steve Bannon Contempt Conviction
frozen_original.synopsis: Steve Bannon, Trump's former chief strategist, had been convicted in November 2022 of two misdemeanor counts of contempt of Congress after defying a subpoena from the House Select Committee investigating January 6. He served four months in federal prison in 2024. After Trump returned to office, the DOJ began systematically dismantling the conviction. In June 2025, the DOJ dropped a separate civil lawsuit that had sought to recover hundreds of presidential records Bannon improperly retained on his personal ProtonMail account, dismissing the case without explanation despite years of litigation and a December 2024 Supreme Court refusal to hear Bannon's appeal. In September 2025, the DOJ formally stopped defending Bannon's contempt conviction before the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, filing a brief stating it is no longer taking the same position as the prior administration. The D.C. Circuit declined to appoint an independent attorney to defend the conviction and ultimately, in April 2026, the Supreme Court sent Bannon's case back to the lower court where the DOJ had filed a motion to dismiss his indictment entirely. On April 6, 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the D.C. Circuit's ruling and remanded for the indictment dismissal to be processed. The episode removed the only accountability Bannon had faced for obstructing congressional oversight of the worst domestic attack on American democracy in modern history.

primary.title: Supreme Court Remands Bannon Case for Further Consideration
primary.description_short: The Supreme Court vacated the judgment under review in Bannon’s case and remanded it in light of a pending motion to dismiss the indictment.
primary.description_medium: On April 6, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court granted Steve Bannon’s petition, vacated the D.C. Circuit judgment, and remanded the case for further consideration in light of a pending motion to dismiss the indictment. The docket records a remand; it does not say the indictment was dismissed or that the conviction was set aside.
primary.description_long: On April 6, 2026, the Supreme Court granted Steve Bannon’s petition, vacated the judgment under review, and remanded the case for further consideration in light of a pending motion to dismiss the indictment. The Court’s docket identifies the lower court as the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit and records that its decision was dated May 10, 2024, with rehearing denied on May 27, 2025. The Supreme Court docket later records that judgment issued on May 8, 2026. These entries describe the case’s path through appellate review and its return for further consideration. They do not show that the district court granted the motion to dismiss, that the indictment was dismissed, or that Bannon’s conviction was overturned. The original entry also joined this criminal case to a separate civil presidential-records lawsuit and characterized the government’s actions as dismantling accountability. This narrower account records only the docketed Supreme Court action and leaves those other claims outside the supported copy.

frozen_original.title: Khamenei Vows Revenge — 'Gates of Hell' Statement
frozen_original.synopsis: Following the destruction of Iran's nuclear facilities by US and Israeli forces in June 2025, Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei delivered a televised address declaring that Iran had 'opened the gates of hell' for its enemies and vowed that revenge against the United States and Israel would be 'severe and unrelenting.' Khamenei's statement was accompanied by declarations of national mourning and calls for regional allies and proxy forces to join the fight. Hezbollah, Iraqi Shia militias, and other Iran-backed groups were placed on operational alert. Intelligence assessments warned of potential terrorist attacks against US interests globally, prompting the State Department to issue worldwide travel alerts and the closure of several US embassies.

primary.title: Khamenei Rejects Trump’s Surrender Demand and Warns Against U.S. Intervention
primary.description_short: Khamenei rejected Trump’s surrender demand and warned of damage if the U.S. entered the conflict.
primary.description_medium: An Associated Press report published by PBS on June 18, 2025, said Ayatollah Ali Khamenei rejected President Donald Trump’s call for Iran’s unconditional surrender and warned that U.S. military involvement would cause “irreparable damage.” The report says Khamenei delivered the remarks in recorded video during Israeli strikes. This corrected draft omits the unsupported “gates of hell” and “severe and unrelenting” quotations.
primary.description_long: On June 18, 2025, Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei rejected U.S. President Donald Trump’s demand for Iran’s unconditional surrender and warned that any U.S. military involvement would cause “irreparable damage,” according to an Associated Press report carried by PBS News. The report says Khamenei made the remarks in a recorded video aired by Iranian state television as Israeli strikes continued. It describes the address as Khamenei’s second public appearance since the strikes began and notes that Trump’s surrender demand came the previous day. This account corrects the frozen card’s June 15 date and narrows its claims to the remarks supported by the accessed report. The source does not support attributing “gates of hell” or a vow of “severe and unrelenting” revenge to Khamenei; those phrases are removed. Search results located “gates of hell” wording attributed to other Iranian figures, so that language is not reassigned to Khamenei. The reporting supports his rejection of the surrender demand and his conditional warning about U.S. military intervention. It does not establish the frozen card’s claims about proxy forces, global travel alerts, embassy closures, or a U.S. strike already having occurred before these June 18 remarks.
primary.date_basis: Statement date in the AP/PBS report.

frozen_original.title: Bondi DOJ Investigates Georgia DA Fani Willis for Trump RICO Prosecution
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, the Trump DOJ under Pam Bondi opened a federal investigation into Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis — who had indicted Trump and 18 co-defendants in a sweeping Georgia RICO case over efforts to overturn the 2020 election — examining her use of county funds and her personal relationship with a prosecutor on the case, the same relationship that had been litigated in Georgia state court and resolved without disqualification. The federal investigation was opened by an administration that had every interest in destroying the Georgia prosecution, using federal prosecutorial power to pile on existing state-level attacks on a prosecutor. Multiple federal judges and former prosecutors described the investigation as an unconstitutional interference with a state criminal proceeding and an abuse of executive power. The Georgia case, already burdened by state-level challenges and Trump's election to the presidency, was further disrupted.

primary.title: Draft Only: Unverified Claim of a Bondi DOJ Probe of Fani Willis
primary.description_short: The supplied record alleges a February 2025 DOJ probe of Fani Willis; the specific investigation and its stated scope remain unverified.
primary.description_medium: The supplied entry alleges that Bondi’s DOJ opened a federal investigation into Fulton County DA Fani Willis in February 2025, examining county spending and her relationship with a prosecutor in the Trump RICO case. The packet provides no source for that specific probe or its alleged purpose. A reported DOJ working-group directive is a separate action and does not verify this claim.
primary.description_long: The frozen entry alleges that the Department of Justice under Attorney General Pam Bondi opened a federal investigation into Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis in February 2025. It says investigators examined county spending and Willis’s personal relationship with a prosecutor in the Georgia prosecution of Donald Trump, and it frames the inquiry as an effort to disrupt that state case. These claims come from the supplied record and are not established facts. The source packet provides no DOJ notice, case number, named investigator, or on-record statement establishing such a probe. During research, ABC News separately reported that Bondi’s February 5 directive established a working group to review actions of state and federal officials who investigated Trump. The article covers that directive and its stated review topics; it does not identify a separate investigation into Willis’s county spending or relationship with a prosecutor. A general review of Trump prosecutions cannot prove that a distinct Willis probe occurred, and a report’s omission does not prove no probe existed. The alleged date, scope, target, motive, legal assessments, and effect on the Georgia RICO case remain unresolved. This internal draft preserves the supplied allegation without reporting it as a verified DOJ action, judicial finding, or proof of retaliatory intent. It is not eligible for publication.
primary.date_status: February 1 is the supplied date only and is not independently verified.
primary.subcategory: Alleged Federal Retaliation Against a Prosecutor

The bank's primary function is to hold and manage assets, including cryptocurrency. This has led to questions about Trump's potential conflicts of interest and the impact on the financial system.
